summary: Describes Synonymous Flow Labels, a method for identifying flows in MPLS networks by using extra labels that behave exactly like the original ones. These synonyms act as flow identifiers that can trigger things like performance measurement of the flow, answering the need set out in RFC 8372.

plainLanguage.summary: Give a group of packets a second name tag that works the same as their first, so you can count and time just that group.

questions: how to identify flows in mpls
what is a synonymous flow label
how do sfl work in mpls
how to measure packet loss in mpls
subtitle: Give MPLS packets a second label that behaves like the original but also triggers an agreed action, such as counting.

tldr.problem: MPLS has no built-in way to tell flows apart, so a router at the far end cannot easily count or inspect one particular flow of packets. RFC 8372 set out the need for flow identities in MPLS.
tldr.mechanism: A Synonymous Flow Label (SFL) is a label that causes exactly the same behavior at the egress router as the label it replaces, plus one or more extra actions agreed in advance between the two edge routers.
tldr.outcome: Operators can trigger per-flow actions, for example packet counting for loss measurement, without changing the packet-forwarding system. The RFC leaves the way SFLs are obtained to other documents.

facts.label: Core idea
facts.value: Label that behaves like another label plus agreed extra actions

today: RFC 8957 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. The way SFLs are requested is left to a separate control protocol, which the RFC cites only as a work in progress.

sections.title: Flow Identity in MPLS
sections.content:
RFC 8372 describes why the MPLS architecture needs flow identities. This document answers with a technique called Synonymous Flow Labels (SFLs): labels that mimic the behavior of other MPLS labels and, by doing so, provide the identification service.

The identifier is used to trigger per-flow operations on the packet at the receiving label switching router. The document is a framework: it describes how SFLs sit in the label stack and what to watch for, not how they are requested.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine every letter in a mailbag looks the same. This RFC suggests a special stamp that does not change where the letter goes, but tells the post office to tally it.

sections.title: What a Synonymous Flow Label Is
sections.content:
An SFL causes exactly the same behavior at the egress Label Edge Router (LER) as the label it replaces, except that it also causes one or more additional actions, previously agreed between the peer LERs, to be run on the packet. Examples given are measuring the number of received packets in a flow, triggering an IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) capture, triggering other deep packet inspection, or identifying the packet source.

In a performance monitoring application, the agreed action could be incrementing a packet counter. The RFC notes this is a natural action in many MPLS implementations, and where supported it permits high-quality packet loss measurement without any change to the packet-forwarding system.

SFLs need to be allocated from the platform label table.
sections.plainLanguage: An SFL is a nickname for a label. Mail with the nickname goes to the same place, but the post office also makes a tally mark.

sections.title: Three Ways to Use SFLs
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three cases.

  • Pseudowire: two labels synonymous with the PW labels are obtained from the egress terminating provider edge. Alternating between these SFLs in place of the PW label lets the packets be batched for counting with no impact on PW forwarding. Strictly only one SFL is needed, but that is an implementor's optimization.
  • Multipoint to point, such as a VPN: the SFLs are made source specific, so batches from one source are marked differently from another. Each ingress LER establishes its own SFL to identify its subflow.
  • No application label (IP over an LSP): an SFL synonymous with the LSP label would create network-wide forwarding state, which is not acceptable for scaling reasons. So an additional label is introduced. With penultimate hop popping (PHP) its semantics can be similar to the LSP label; without PHP they are similar to an MPLS Explicit NULL.

How the extra labels are obtained is outside the scope of the text. One control protocol for it is described in an Internet-Draft the RFC cites as a work in progress.
sections.plainLanguage: You can use the nickname label in place of a normal label, one per sender, or as an extra label when there was nothing to nickname.

sections.title: Label Stacks in the Data Plane
sections.content:
With an application label present, the SFL replaces it in the stack. The LSP label above it may be removed by PHP. At the egress LER the LSP label is popped if present, then the SFL is processed, running both the synonymous function and the application's own function.

With a single-label stack, the ingress LER first pushes the SFL and then pushes the LSP label. At the receiver, if the LSP label is still there it is processed normally and popped, revealing the SFL. For the measurements defined in RFC 6374 the SFL is simply counted and discarded, like an MPLS Explicit NULL, and the IP packet after it is processed as normal. If the LSP label was removed by PHP upstream, the SFL can be treated either as an LSP label that was not PHPed or as an Explicit NULL with SFL actions. For the measurement system described, the two are indistinguishable, so either may be implemented.

The TTL and Traffic Class bits in the SFL label stack entry would normally be set to the same values as in the label it is synonymous with. They MAY be set to other values if there is an application need, for instance to make the SFL trigger an action in the TTL expiry exception path.
sections.plainLanguage: The special label rides in the same stack of labels as usual. The last router peels off the outer one, then reads the special one, counts it and carries on.

sections.title: Aggregating SFL Actions
sections.content:
Sometimes one action should cover many labels, for example one counter for a group of application labels, or an application that uses so many labels that allocating an SFL for each would not be viable. Then an additional label is placed in the stack as an aggregate instruction.

This is not strictly synonymous, because the SFL does not replace an existing label. It resembles the single-label case, and the same signaling, management and configuration tools apply. The aggregate SFL may come before or after the application label; the choice is application specific and depends on whether the action needs the full application context and whether finding an SFL after the application label would complicate the application.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have lots of labels, one shared tally stamp can count them all together instead of giving every label its own.

sections.title: Equal-Cost Multipath Effects
sections.content:
Adding an SFL to an existing flow may make it take a different path through the network under Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP). That can invalidate uses of the SFL such as performance measurement, because the measured packets no longer travel the path of the ones that are not measured.

The RFC offers two remedies. The operator MAY always run with the SFL in the label stack. Or the operator can use entropy labels (RFC 6790) in a network that fully supports this kind of ECMP. In that case the intervening MPLS network MUST NOT load balance on any packet field other than the entropy label, which the RFC notes is stricter than the text in Section 4.3 of RFC 6790.
sections.plainLanguage: If adding the special label makes a packet take a different road, your count would be about the wrong road. So keep the label on always, or make sure the roads are picked the same way.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Carrying originating or flow information in a packet gives an observer more identity information, so it can degrade privacy. It does not by itself say which node originated the packet unless the attacker can inspect the network at the point of ingress or inspect the control protocol packets. The RFC suggests mitigation by encrypting control protocol packets, regularly changing the synonymous labels, using several labels at once, or a combination. Where IPFIX or other deep packet inspection is used, their privacy considerations apply as well.

On security, the RFC says there are no new security issues associated with the MPLS data plane. Any control protocol used to request SFLs needs to check that the requesting node is authorized by the network operator. There are no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: A special tag could help a snoop learn more about your traffic. Changing tags often, and only letting approved routers ask for them, helps keep things private.
